12 Three coplanar forces act on an object in the directions shown.
In which diagram could the object be in equilibrium?
A
B
C
D

hints: Extend each arrow in diagram A, B, C and D into a full straight line in both directions and look for where the three lines cross.
Recall that three non-parallel coplanar forces in equilibrium must be concurrent - all three lines of action must pass through one common point so resultant force and resultant moment are zero.
Compare the crossing points: in only one diagram do the top, lower-left and right lines all cross together, allowing a closed $F_1 + F_2 + F_3 = 0$ triangle.
walkthrough: Identify the equilibrium rule for this item: for three coplanar forces that are not parallel, the lines of action must be concurrent and the vectors must add to zero.

Extend the lines: in A the two top inward pushes and the bottom outward push intersect pairwise at different places, not at one point. In B the outward top-left force and the two inward forces also give three separate intersections.
In D the left inward horizontal force and the right outward horizontal force both act to the right, so they cannot cancel, and the lower outward force line does not pass through their line.
In C the downward force from the top, the up-right force from the lower left, and the down-right force from the right can all be extended to cross at one region inside the object.
Concurrent lines allow the forces to be slid to a common point where their vector sum can be zero with no resultant moment, forming a closed triangle. This is option C

A.explanation: The lines of action of the two upper inward forces and the lower outward force do not meet at one common point, so the three forces cannot be concurrent.

B.explanation: The lines of action extended forward and backward form three separate intersections, so there is a net force and a net moment.

C.explanation: The three lines of action can meet at a single concurrent point, allowing the vector sum to be zero with a closed force triangle.

D.explanation: Two forces both point to the right and are offset, so they add rather than cancel and their lines cannot all meet at one point with the third force.
